sec.title: Background
sec.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs) and other H3K27M-mutated diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs) are brain tumors that primarily affect children. Radiotherapy is the standard of care but only provides only temporary symptomatic relief due to radioresistance. Although hypoxia is a major driver of radioresistance in other tumors, there is no definitive evidence that DIPGs are hypoxic. Diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas often contain histone mutations, which alter tumor metabolism and are also associated with radioresistance. Our objective was to identify the metabolic profiles of DIPG cells, detect hypoxia signatures, and uncover metabolism-linked mechanisms of radioresistance to improve tumor radiosensitivity.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: Using DIPG models combined with clinical datasets, we examined mitochondrial metabolism and signatures of hypoxia. We explored DIPG reliance on mitochondrial metabolism using extracellular flux assays and targeted metabolomics. In vitro and in vivo models were used to explore the mechanisms of targeting mitochondrial bioenergetics and hypoxia for radiosensitization. Treatment-induced transcriptomics and metabolomics were also investigated.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: Comprehensive analyses of DIPG cells show signatures of enhanced oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS). We also identified increased expression of specific OXPHOS-related genes and signatures of hypoxia gene expression in datasets obtained from DIPG patients. We found the presence of hypoxia in orthotopic mouse models bearing DIPG tumors. These findings enabled us to develop a proof-of-concept treatment strategy to enhance radiosensitivity of DIPGs in vitro and in animal models.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma cells rely on mitochondrial metabolism for growth, and targeting mitochondria disrupts bioenergetics, alleviates hypoxia, and enhances radiosensitivity. These findings warrant further exploration of OXPHOS inhibition as a radiosensitizing strategy for DIPG treatment.
Keywords: diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas, hypoxia, mitochondria, radiotherapy

list-item.p: Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) tumors exhibit heterogeneity in their metabolic activities, but mitochondrial metabolism is the primary pathway for ATP production.
Enhanced mitochondrial respiration may be leading to hypoxia in DIPG tumors, which can be targeted to effectively improve radiosensitivity in vitro and in vivo.
Under the therapeutic pressure of mitochondrial inhibition, DIPG cells transcriptionally increase cholesterol synthesis pathways and show widespread metabolic disruption.

boxed-text.p: This study is the first to characterize diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma (DIPG) cells in their glucose metabolism pathways and demonstrate the existence of hypoxia in DIPG models, supported by in vitro, in vivo, and clinical data. Diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas’ reliance on mitochondrial metabolism and oxidative phosphorylation can increase hypoxia, but this can be effectively reduced using mitochondrial inhibitors such as biguanides. RNA-sequencing and metabolomics studies showed that DIPG tumors with suppressed mitochondrial function switch to alternative metabolic pathways, such as cholesterol synthesis, to compensate for the metabolic disruption. These insights could be utilized to develop new combination therapeutic strategies to enhance the efficacy of radiotherapy, the only standard treatment, for rapid clinical translation and patient benefit in DIPG.

body.p: Diffuse midline gliomas (DMGs), including diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas (DIPGs), are aggressive brain tumors that typically occur in children. Radiotherapy is the standard treatment, but it provides only temporary symptomatic relief. Nearly all DIPG patients relapse within a year due to radioresistance. Therefore, understanding radioresistance mechanisms and identifying novel therapeutic avenues will be critical to improving overall survival rates.

Approximately, 70-85% of DIPGs harbor mutations in histone H3, resulting in a substitution of lysine 27 with methionine (H3K27M).1–3 This mutation causes global hypomethylation of H3K27 and reprogramming of tumor metabolism to enhance tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycling and oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS).4 Many cancer cells have an enhanced reliance on mitochondrial metabolism and OXPHOS to facilitate their proliferation and survival.5 The heightened oxygen demand from OXPHOS, combined with inadequate vascularization, can lead to regions of hypoxia, commonly seen in other tumors.6 Although tumor hypoxia has never been directly observed or quantified in DIPGs, clinical observations have demonstrated low blood perfusion and necrotic regions, characteristics associated with hypoxic tumors.7 Hypoxia contributes to aggressive tumor behavior and treatment resistance in other cancers.8,9 Hypoxia also reduces the efficacy of radiation by reducing molecular oxygen which acts as a reactive electrophile that induces DNA damage, and through mechanisms involving hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and others.10

Our first aim was to identify cellular metabolism requirements within DIPGs and determine its correlation with cell doubling rates and responsiveness to radiation. We also examined clinical DIPG samples and mouse models to find signatures of hypoxia and mitochondrial respiration. Our initial findings guided our selection of drugs to enhance the radiosensitivity of DIPG cells by targeting mitochondrial metabolism and hypoxia. The transcriptional and metabolic alterations post-treatment were then measured to determine the mechanism of radiosensitization.

sec.title: Materials and Methods
sec.p: Experimental details are described briefly below and in more detail in Supplementary File. See Supplementary Table 1 for patient cohort and tumor sample information.

sec.title: Cell Culture
sec.p: Cell culture conditions are described in Supplementary File.

sec.title: Extracellular Flux Assays
sec.p: Oxygen consumption rate (OCR) and extracellular acidification rate (ECAR) were determined using an XF Extracellular Flux Analyzer (Agilent). XF Cell Mito Stress, Glycolysis Stress, and Real-Time ATP rate assays (which measure ATP generated from glycolysis [glycoATP] and the mitochondria [mitoATP]) were performed according to the manufacturer’s instructions. To confirm drugs inhibit Complex I, HSJD-DIPG007 were treated for 3 h and OCR was measured for each Complex (I-IV).

sec.title: Cell Proliferation Assay
sec.p: Cell proliferation was assessed using MTS assays according to the manufacturer’s protocol.

sec.title: DNA Damage and Apoptosis Assay
sec.p: Cells were treated with phenformin for 6 h followed by radiotherapy, and then collected 30 min later for assessing DNA damage. To assess apoptosis, cells were collected after 24 h of phenformin treatment (18 h following radiation treatment). Proteins were extracted for western blotting and probed for γ-H2AX, cleaved caspase 3, and MCL-1. γ-H2AX was also assessed by confocal microscopy.

sec.title: Orthotopic Animal Models
sec.p: The protocol was approved by the Western Sydney Local Health District Animal Ethics Committee (5185.05.23). Briefly, female athymic nude mice (Balb/c, 6-8 weeks) were intracranially injected either with 4 × 105 SU-DIPG13P* cells or 2 × 105 HSJD-DIPG007 cells in the fourth ventricle/pons region using the coordinates: 6 mm posterior, 0.5 mm lateral, and 3.5 mm below the bregma. Mice at endpoint showing tumor-related neurological symptoms were euthanized. Three mice from each group at endpoint were anesthetized with isoflurane followed by measuring oxygen levels in their brain using the oxygen microsensor PM-PSt7 (PreSens). Upon finishing, these mice were euthanized by overdosing isoflurane followed by cervical dislocation. Brains were excised following termination for immunohistochemistry (see Supplementary File).

For treatments, mice were randomly divided into 4 groups of 7: control, phenformin, radiotherapy, and combination. Phenformin was administered by gavage at 125 mg/kg once daily, starting from day 21 after tumor inoculation for 12 days. Mice in control and radiotherapy-alone arms received distilled water. Radiation was delivered using XRad 320 to the whole brain of the mouse, with the entire body being covered by a lead shield (Precision). The total radiation dose administered was 10 Gy at a clinically relevant 2 Gy/fraction schedule on a 5-day schedule from day 28 to day 32.

sec.title: Clinical Datasets
sec.p: To assess mRNA expression within cohorts of specific pediatric brain tumor subtypes, we used the pediatric cBioportal tool11,12 to download mRNA expression data for the major histological types of pediatric brain cancer from the Open Pediatric Cancer (OpenPedCan) Project v12 dataset (data downloaded on September 28, 2023) and the v15 dataset (data downloaded on May 30, 2024, and August 12, 2024). These data consisted of tumor samples from 167 glioblastoma (GBM) samples from 159 patients, 12 brainstem glioma DIPGs from 12 patients, 411 DMG-H3K27M samples from 224 patients, 246 caudate (basal ganglia, GTEx), 255 nontumor brain cortex (GTEx), and 202 nontumor hypothalamus samples. RNA data were not available for all samples/patients. Specific to brainstem glioma DIPGs and DMG-H3K27M: 423 samples were analyzed from 235 patients (128 females, 102 males, and 5 unreported/unknown) with an average age of 8.1 years. Ages for other tumor subtypes, as well as other individual anonymous patient characteristics (gender, survival status, cancer type, patient ID, sample ID age, and race), are provided in Supplementary File. Normal brain tissue mRNA levels were taken from GTEx data already incorporated and normalized into Pediatric cBioportal. Mitochondrial Complex I gene expression scores were created by the sum of log2 z-score expression for 37 genes encoding Complex I proteins in the human genome. Hypoxia scores were created by using the sum of log2 z-score expression for the 50 genes described in the hypoxia Buffa metagene score.13 See Supplementary Table 1 for further details.

sec.title: Metabolomics
sec.p: Cells were treated with drugs for 24 h followed by Phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) wash and metabolite extraction (1:1 methanol:water, followed by chloroform). The aqueous layer phase was transferred, and samples dried before rehydrating with water and acetone-nitrile mix. The mixer was vortexed and centrifuged. The supernatant was used for liquid chromatography-coupled tandem mass spectrometry (LC-MS/MS)-targeted metabolomics with HILIC or AMIDE column. Metaboanalyst 5.0 was used for analysis. See Supplementary File for more details.

sec.title: RNA Sequencing
sec.p: Cells were collected 24 h post-treatment and RNA was extracted. High-quality total RNA (RIN > 8) was used for the Illumina Truseq stranded mRNA library preparation kit and then sequenced on the Illumina Novaseq 6000 platform using the SP flow cell with single-end 100 bp reads. For further details, see Supplementary File.

sec.title: Statistical Analysis
sec.p: Statistical analysis was performed with GraphPad Prism. Data are presented as the mean ± SD and all experiments were repeated at least twice in 3-5 replicates per condition. Direct comparison between 2 groups was examined using an unpaired two-tailed Student’s t-test. Ordinary one-way ANOVA was conducted for multigroup comparisons followed by a post-hoc Dunnett’s test (groups compared with one control group) or post-hoc Tukey’s test (to identify differences among subgroups) where appropriate. P-values of <0.05 (two-sided) were considered statistically significant.

sec.title: Patient-Derived DIPG Cell Lines Use OXPHOS Combined with Glycolysis to Sustain Their Growth
sec.p: Because H3K27M mutations alter metabolism,4 we hypothesized that DIPGs increase mitochondrial respiration to support proliferation. To assess this, we measured ATP production rates in 8 patient-derived DIPG cell lines with H3K27M mutations (SU-DIPG6, 13P*, 17, 21, 24, HSJD-DIPG007, 012, and 013) and compared with immortalized human fetal astrocytes (hTERT IHA). The XF Real-Time ATP Rate Assay measures ATP specifically generated from glycolysis (glycoATP) and the mitochondria (mitoATP). We grouped DIPG cell lines into 4 energetic profiles (Figure 1A): quiescent (SU-DIPG13P*, 21, and HSJD-DIPG013), glycolytic (HSJD-DIPG007), aerobic (SU-DIPG6, HSJD-DIPG012), and energetic (both higher mitoATP and glycoATP:SU-DIPG17, 24). All cell lines utilized both glycolysis and OXPHOS to produce ATP. Analyses of the percentage of mitoATP and glycoATP production showed that SU-DIPG13P*, 21, and HSJD-DIPG007 use both glycolysis and OXPHOS equally, while the rest showed a preference for OXPHOS. SU-DIPG6 and HSJD-DIPG012 produced more than 75% of ATP from OXPHOS (Figure 1B). In contrast to most DIPG cell lines, fetal astrocytes were quiescent (Figure 1A), and astrocytes had the highest percentage of glycoATP, with the lowest percentage of mitoATP of all cell lines (Figure 1B).

sec.title: Increased OXPHOS, Glycolysis, and ATP Correlate with Faster Proliferation
sec.p: To examine whether faster proliferation is associated with OXPHOS/glycolysis, we measured the cell doubling time and correlated this with basal OCR or extracellular acidification rate (ECAR). Growth rates were variable, ranging from SU-DIPG17 at ~14 h doubling time to HSJD-DIPG013 at ~80 h (Figure 1C). The most energetic cells, generally, were the most rapidly proliferating cell lines. The fastest growing SU-DIPG17 was also the most energetic, exhibiting the highest mitoATP. In contrast, the most quiescent cell line SU-DIPG13P* maintained low mitoATP and glycoATP production relative to most of the other cell lines. Basal respiration rates correlated with total ATP production (Figure 1D). Cell lines with higher rates of basal respiration had higher rates of proliferation in vitro (Figure 1E). Similarly, higher levels of total ATP production resulted in higher rates of proliferation in vitro (Figure 1F) (XF real-time data shown in Supplementary Figure 1).

sec.title: DIPG Patient Tumors Have Increased OXPHOS-Related Gene Expression in Clinical Samples and Cell Lines
sec.p: Some tumors rely on OXPHOS for energy, and increased oxygen consumption can cause localized hypoxia. Tumors can increase OXPHOS flux by overexpressing genes involved in the process. Increased expression of these genes correlates with increased OXPHOS activity in vivo.14 We observed high OXPHOS rates in DIPG cells in vitro (Figure 1); therefore, we assessed OXPHOS gene expression in DIPG tumors and patient-derived cell lines. We were interested in electron transport chain (ETC) genes, where clinically approved drugs are known to target the protein product. We used datasets from the Childhood Cancer Model Atlas (CCMA),15 cBioPortal,11,12, and the Open Pediatric Cancer (OpenPedCan) Project v15 to extract mRNA abundance for cell lines and patients under multiple pediatric (≤21 years old) brain tumor classifications (brainstem glioma [BSG] DIPG and DMG-H3K27M). One patient within the DMG-H3K27M classification was 29 years old. We also extracted data for adult GBMs (21-85 years old) for comparison. We used mRNA expression data from nontumor brain tissue samples (GTEx) and nonmalignant brain cell lines (CCMA). We used these data to create a mitochondrial Complex I expression score from the normalized log2 mRNA values of the 37 Complex I structural genes encoded in the human (nuclear) genome.14

Complex I gene expression scores significantly increased for BSG-DIPG and DMG-H3K27M tumors, but not in GBM, when compared with the nontumor brain (caudate) (Figure 2A). An interesting pattern emerged from the data on Complex I expression for pediatric brain tumor subtypes. Complex I gene expression scores appeared to fall into two or more groups of high and low expression (Figure 2A). This pattern was not seen in the GBMs. We have highlighted this pattern across patient samples and across different Complex I genes in the heatmap for the DMG-H3K27M tumors (Figure 2B). The importance of this pattern is unclear; however, this would align with the in vitro data obtained from patient-derived cell lines where we observed a range of OXPHOS utilization. Using the RNA-sequencing data from CCMA, we created Complex I gene expression scores for available DIPG cell lines, as well as nontumor cell lines (NHB, NSC). All DIPG cell lines had higher Complex I scores than nontumor cell lines (Figure 1G). There was not a clear pattern between Complex I gene expression scores in individual DIPG cell lines and their basal respiration levels.

sec.title: DIPG Clinical Samples Show Evidence of Hypoxic Gene Expression Signatures
sec.p: If DIPG tumors have increased OXPHOS in vivo, as demonstrated in our in vitro experiments, tumors would consume a significant amount of oxygen, creating hypoxic regions. Hypoxia is common in tumors like GBM,8 although the cause of hypoxia may vary between tumor types. While OXPHOS requires oxygen to function, the ETC continues to function optimally at oxygen concentrations as low as 0.5% v/v.16 While there are limited in vivo data on DIPG hypoxia, there are established methods for assessing tumor hypoxia, including the Buffa hypoxia signature, which comprises a list of 50 genes that are commonly overexpressed in hypoxic tumors when compared with surrounding nontumor tissue.13 Similar to the Complex I gene expression analyses, we used the same publicly available datasets11,12 to evaluate expression of the Buffa hypoxia metagene signature (50 genes that are prognostic of hypoxia in human tumors).13 To generate a hypoxia score, the data for all 50 genes were combined in a single score for each tumor sample extracted from cBioPortal11,12 and the Open Pediatric Cancer (OpenPedCan) Project v15, as described in the previous section and in Supplementary File. All 3 tumor subtypes had a significantly increased hypoxia score when compared with the caudate (Figure 2C). We also observed a strong correlation between the hypoxia metagene score and the Complex I gene expression score for individual tumors or normal brain tissue samples (Figure 2D). These data indicate that DIPG tumors with higher Complex I score show gene expression patterns consistent with a hypoxic tumor microenvironment, although the underlying tumor genetics may affect expression in varying ways.

sec.title: DIPG Orthotopic Xenograft Mouse Models Show Hypoxic Gene Signatures
sec.p: We next examined whether hypoxia was present in DIPG mouse models. Patient-derived cell lines SU-DIPG13P* and HSJD-DIPG007 are commonly used in orthotopic models. SU-DIPG13P* cells were injected into the brainstem, and cells migrated in a diffuse pattern mimicking what is seen in human patients (Figure 2E, top row). We used immunohistochemistry to probe for the hypoxia markers, HIF-1α, and vascular endothelial growth factor A (VEGFA) in brain slices containing both SU-DIPG13P* tumor cells and normal mouse brain tissue. On histological slides, HIF-1α is consistently expressed within the tumor cells (Figure 2E, bottom row). Furthermore, we could see colocalized staining of VEGFA in areas of the tumor (Figure 2E, middle row).

A separate cohort of mice with orthotopic HSJD-DIPG007 tumors were injected with the 2-nitroimidazole EF-5 and pimonidazole, which are hypoxia imaging markers that selectively bind to hypoxic cells. We also stained for H3K27M mutations to identify tumor cells (Figure 2F). As expected, tumor cell growth was more diffuse for this model, with most tumor cells in the pons and cerebellum. In contrast, with SU-DIPG13P* model, HSJD-DIPG007 tumor cells migrate further from their initial injection site and invade the frontal lobes, showing a very invasive growth pattern (Figure 2F, top row). EF-5 and pimonidazole-positive staining can be found in the areas in the brain where the tumor cells are also positively stained with H3K27M (Figure 2F, middle and bottom rows).

To determine oxygen levels within orthotopic xenograft tumors, we used a high-resolution oxygen electrode needle (Presens) to measure oxygenation at various depths of the brain. Mice reaching endpoint were put under deep anesthesia using isoflurane. The needle was inserted using the KOPF stereotactic frame with the same coordinates used for cell implantation. Oxygen measurements were taken at depths of 3.5 mm (the same depth as the initial tumor cell injection), 3 mm, 2 mm, and 1 mm. As shown in Figure 2G, free oxygen levels were distributed in a wide range, with higher average levels seen at a 1 mm depth and lower levels at 3 mm depth. There was a range of oxygenation levels within the general tumor area which are reflective of previously published values for the brain.17

sec.title: Blocking Mitochondrial Function and OXPHOS in DIPG Cells with Biguanides Reduces Tumor Cell Viability and Oxygen Consumption
sec.p: We next assessed whether Complex I inhibitors impact DIPG cell proliferation. Metformin and phenformin are biguanides that inhibit Complex I, decreasing OXPHOS and growth in cancer cell lines.18 We tested metformin, the first-line biguanide for the treatment of type 2 diabetes, and phenformin, a more potent biguanide derivative (withdrawn from the market due to a higher risk of acidosis), for its efficacy in inhibiting DIPG growth. These drugs penetrate the blood-brain barrier,19 making them potential candidates to be tested in vivo. We measured DIPG cell viability following drug treatment and observed a dose-dependent effect (Figure 3A; Supplementary Figure 2A). Phenformin was ~20-100 times more potent than metformin across all 8 DIPG cell lines. SU-DIPG13P* was the most sensitive cell line to phenformin/metformin whilst HSJD-DIPG012 was the most resistant one (Supplementary Figure 2A). The sensitivity of DIPG cells to metformin is closely correlated to their sensitivity to phenformin, suggesting that these 2 biguanides have a similar mechanism of action in DIPG cells (Supplementary Figure 2B).

sec.p: We next examined whether biguanides inhibit OCR in SU-DIPG17 cells. Both metformin and phenformin showed a dose-dependent inhibitory effect on OCR, while an increase in ECAR was also observed (Figure 3B). To confirm that phenformin and metformin inhibit Complex I in DIPG cells, we treated HSJD-DIPG007 cells with these drugs for 3 h and measured specific OCR of each Complex (I-IV). Both phenformin and metformin inhibited Complex I activity, whereas Complex II, III, and IV were unaffected (Figure 3C; Supplementary Figure 2C). As phenformin was more potent than metformin, the following experiments were carried out using phenformin only.

To study the effect of phenformin on the mitochondria in DIPG cells, XF Cell Mito Stress and Real-Time ATP Rate Assays were carried out. A dose-dependent inhibitory effect was observed in all mitochondrial parameters (Figure 3D). Phenformin also decreased the ATP rate index by inhibiting mitoATP and reducing total ATP production (Figure 3E, F; Supplementary Figure 2D). AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) acts as a cellular sensor of low intracellular ATP and it is rapidly activated by increased AMP, which we observed in our metabolomics analysis (Figure 5A). Inhibition of Complex I by phenformin did activate AMPK in DIPG cells, as measured by AMPK-phosphorylation (Figure 3G).

sec.title: Phenformin Reduces Hypoxia in Neurospheres and Enhances Radiation Sensitivity in DIPG Cells by Reducing Hypoxia, Inducing DNA Double-Strand Breaks, and Increasing Apoptosis In Vitro
sec.p: We quantified the radiosensitivity of DIPG cells by measuring the surviving fraction of cells treated with a single 2 Gy of radiation (SF2). SU-DIPG21 had the highest radiosensitivity and SU-DIPG13P* was the most radioresistant (Figure 4A). There was no correlation between SF2 and XF bioenergetic parameters (data not shown). To measure the effect of phenformin on radiosensitivity, we pretreated HSJD-DIPG007 neurospheres (which form hypoxic cores) with phenformin, exposed them to radiotherapy, and plated them in soft agar for colony-forming assays. Unlike monolayers, neurospheres mimic the oxygen and nutrient gradients in tumors in vivo, with a hypoxic core forming in spheroids larger than 200 μm.20 As shown in Figure 4B, HSJD-DIPG007 cells were more sensitive to radiation when pretreated with phenformin.

sec.p: To determine whether phenformin is effectively reducing hypoxia, two 3D neurosphere models using HSJD-DIPG007 and SU-DIPG6 cells were used. We used an Image-iT Green Hypoxia Dye to identify regions of hypoxia in live neurospheres. It is nonfluorescent when live cells are normoxic and becomes fluorescent when oxygen levels decrease below 5% vol/vol. After phenformin, hypoxia reduction was observed in both models (Figure 4C), and this was corroborated by a dose-dependent reduction in HIF-1α (Figure 4D). In line with the hypoxia inhibitory effect, phenformin-treated HSJD-DIPG007 showed reduced expression of the Buffa hypoxia metagene score (from RNASeq, Figure 4E).

To confirm phenformin enhances radiosensitivity in a wider range of cell lines, we used a combination of clonogenic assays, viability assays, and live cell analysis of neurospheres. We found that HSJD-DIPG013 (Supplementary Figure 3A), SU-DIPG13P* (Supplementary Figure 3B), and SU-DIPG6 (Supplementary Figure 3C) were all more sensitive to the combination of phenformin and radiation when compared with the control group or either treatment alone.

To explore whether radiosensitization is due to hypoxia reduction, we performed a liquid colony-forming assay that used SU-DIPG17 as a monolayer, without hypoxia. Surprisingly, we still observed radiosensitization in phenformin-treated cells (Figure 4F). Further experiments demonstrated phenformin-enhanced radiation’s effect on DNA damage and apoptosis in SU-DIPG17 cells, measured by western blots of γ-H2AX, cleaved caspase 3, and MCL-1 (Figure 4G). Confocal microscopy confirmed increased DNA damage through positive γ-H2AX staining (Figure 4H). All these findings indicate that phenformin may work in multiple ways to radiosensitize cells.

sec.title: Phenformin Enhances the Effect of Radiation in Orthotopic In Vivo Models of DIPG, Prolonging Overall Survival
sec.p: To identify whether the radiosensitizing effect of phenformin could prolong survival, we used a mouse model bearing HSJD-DIPG007 tumors. Figure 4I demonstrates the schedule of tumor inoculation followed by phenformin and radiation treatments. The aim of this experiment was to determine whether a brief course of phenformin administered with radiation could enhance the effects of radiation. No obvious toxicity was observed from any treatment arm. Although radiation alone (10 Gy) or a brief schedule of phenformin alone (125 mg/kg/day for 12 days) did not significantly delay the onset of symptoms, the combination of phenformin and radiation substantially prolonged the median survival of this model by 14 days (Figure 4J).

sec.title: Reduction of Mitochondrial Metabolism by Phenformin Alters the Transcriptome and Induces Widespread Metabolic Alterations in DIPG Cells
sec.p: Phenformin alters cell metabolism via the inhibition of Complex I and reduces mitochondrial ATP production (Figure 3E). To determine how this impacts DIPG metabolism, we used targeted metabolomics combined with matched RNA sequencing of HSJD-DIPG007 samples to map connections between metabolites and RNA transcripts. Metabolite changes are depicted in the volcano plot (Figure 5A) and the unsupervised hierarchical clustering heatmap displaying fold change of the top 25 profiled metabolites (Figure 5B). Differential expression analysis was used to compare gene expression levels between the HSJD-DIPG007 cells treated with phenformin and control based on the normalized RNASeq counts. There were 787 differentially expressed genes (DEGs), comprising 349 downregulated genes and 438 upregulated genes shown in the unsupervised hierarchical clustering heatmap (Figure 5C).

Many intracellular glycolytic metabolites were decreased by phenformin, including glucose, fructose-1,6-BP (FBP), 3-phospho-glycerate (3PG), and phosphoenolpyruvate (PEP), while glucose-6-phosphate (G6P), fructose-6-phosphate (F6P), and pyruvate and lactate increased. Phenformin has been linked to lactate acidosis5 and we observed this in vitro. The glycolytic ATP rate did not change appreciably when treated with phenformin (Figure 3E), but many glycolytic intermediates showed depletion indicating the cells may be struggling to increase glycolytic flux to compensate for decreased mitochondrial (and total) ATP. Simultaneously, we found decreased expression of glycolytic enzymes in phenformin-treated HSJD-DIPG007 cells (highlighted in Figure 6, including HK2, PGK1, PGAM1, GPI, TPI1, ALDOA, GAPDH, ENO1, and ENO2, also see Supplementary Figure 7), indicating that the cells may be unable to increase glycolytic flux. Metabolomics analysis on phenformin-treated SU-DIPG17 cells showed similar metabolite changes to HSJD-DIPG007 cells, including in glycolysis, TCA cycle, and amino acids (Supplementary Figure 4). In HSJD-DIPG007 cells, citrate, succinyl-CoA, succinate, and NADH decreased, while fumarate, malate, oxaloacetate, and ADP increased, indicating potentially decreased TCA cycling. Expression of many TCA cycle genes did not change, indicating decreased flux of metabolites, rather than decreased enzyme availability. This is supported by XF Cell Mito Stress data, showing that spare respiratory capacity was only slightly reduced with phenformin, while maximal respiration was significantly reduced (Figure 3D). While pyruvate levels increased, a decreased ability to channel pyruvate and α-KG into the TCA cycle likely reduced overall TCA flux, resulting in a decrease in OCR and ATP production (Figure 3).

Increased quantity for a metabolite or RNA is shown in red, while decreases are highlighted in blue. Metabolites or RNAs that were either not measured or did not change are in black.

sec.p: Many intracellular amino acids increased following phenformin treatment (Figure 5A). With decreased ATP, cells may be unable to build cellular structures, leading to no utilization of the building blocks like amino acids. Increased aspartate could stem from the inability of pyruvate to enter the TCA cycle resulting in oxaloacetate being converted to aspartate, rather than combining with acetyl-CoA to form citrate. This is supported by an increase in GOT1 gene expression.

We also performed unbiased searches using the Gene Ontology (GO) (Supplementary Figure 5A) and Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) tools (Figure 5D) to identify the top impacted pathways from RNAseq data. Metabolism pathways were the most highly impacted (Figure 5E; Supplementary Figures 5B and 7), particularly sterol and cholesterol pathways. Other significantly altered transcriptional pathways of interest included cell cycle, HIF-1 signaling, p53 signaling, and transcriptional misregulation in cancer. In the GO (Supplementary Figure 5B) and KEGG pathways (Figure 5E), all genes within steroid biosynthesis and terpenoid synthesis increased. For other highly impacted pathways, there was a mix of upregulated and downregulated genes (Supplementary Figures 5B and 7). Cell cycle and HIF-1 signaling gene expression mostly decreased, and this supports our data showing that phenformin reduced hypoxia in neurospheres (Figure 4C) and decreased cell viability (Figure 3A). The transcriptional response to hypoxia was substantially altered, as well as in lipid and fatty acid metabolism, and metabolic terms linked to glycolysis and the mitochondria. Biosynthesis of amino acids, glycolysis and gluconeogenesis, glycine, serine and threonine pathways, and carbon metabolism were also highly impacted, and this can be visualized in Figure 6 when combined with our metabolomics data.

An unexpected finding was the transcriptomic shift toward expression of genes in cholesterol metabolism upon phenformin treatment (Figure 5C–E; Supplementary Figure 5). Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma cells have increased basal cholesterol metabolism, possibly from p53 mutations, which activate the mevalonate pathway.21 Furthermore, cholesterol synthesis inhibitors have shown preclinical efficacy in these tumors.21 Phenformin upregulated expression of nearly every gene encoding enzymes of the mevalonate and cholesterol synthesis pathway (Figures 5C–E and 6; Supplementary Figures 5 and 7). Our targeted metabolomics platform measures several metabolites in this pathway. Mevalonate and 3-hydroxybutyrate levels were not altered by phenformin and HMG-CoA peak signals were low in both control and phenformin-treated cells (Supplementary Figure 6A). Branched-chain amino acids (valine, leucine, and isoleucine) accumulated following phenformin treatment. This may indicate inefficient cholesterol synthesis due to the widespread disruption of metabolism from phenformin.

While cholesterol synthesis was a significant finding in transcriptomics, some of the largest metabolite changes related to carnitines. Short-chain acylcarnitines including butyrylcarnitine, acetylcarnitine, isovalerylcarnitine, and 2-methylbutyrylcarnitine were all significantly decreased, while CoA and free carnitine increased following phenformin treatment (Figure 5A and B). Carnitine is an important component of mitochondrial and fatty acid metabolism. Previous studies of patients with ovarian tumors, who were also taking metformin, showed that short-chain carnitines decreased within tumors,22 aligning with our in vitro data. Our transcriptomics data also identified changes in fatty acid metabolism with many genes in fatty acid biosynthesis, metabolism, and transport showing increased expression (Supplementary Figure 8). Lipid metabolism may also be impacted with increased dihydroxyacetone phosphate (DHAP) and glycerol-3-phosphate (Gro3P), while the expression of ALDOA and TPI1 decreased. Metformin has previously been found to inhibit mitochondrial respiration of Gro3P, leading to DHAP conversion,23 and this may be occurring with phenformin. Overall, the data in HSJD-DIPG007 cells show widespread metabolic disruption following phenformin.

We also assessed metabolic alterations in radiation-treated HSJD-DIPG007 cells and in phenformin plus radiation-treated cells. Radiation had a minor effect on metabolite levels (Supplementary Figure 6B) and when radiation was combined with phenformin, metabolite changes largely matched the phenformin-only group (at 24 h post-treatment in vitro) (Supplementary Figure 6C). Transcriptomic analysis of radiation-treated HSJD-DIPG007 cells revealed 109 DEGs 24 h after 2 Gy radiation, comprising 20 downregulated genes and 89 upregulated genes shown in the unsupervised hierarchical clustering heatmap (Supplementary Figure 9A). Unbiased pathway analysis found that the p53 signaling pathway was the top impacted pathway (Supplementary Figure 9B) and the top GO terms were primarily related to the DNA damage response (Supplementary Figure 9C). Radiation may not cause substantial metabolism alterations, but radiation is also known to have a delayed effect, and our time points may not have captured the full impact.

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Metabolic reprogramming is a cancer hallmark and can be driven by hypoxia.4 Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma tumors have not been conclusively shown to be hypoxic or normoxic. Diffuse intrinsic pontine glioma tumors with the H3K27M mutation4 undergo metabolic reprogramming, but whether hypoxia plays a role remains unknown. Here we characterized the bioenergetic profiles of DIPG cells and astrocytes. We found that most ATP in DIPGs stems from OXPHOS, while astrocytes derive more ATP through glycolysis. Diffuse intrinsic pontine gliomas increase OXPHOS and ATP to support faster proliferation in vitro. Emerging evidence indicates that proliferating tumor cells have increased mitochondrial respiration relative to quiescent cells.24 We showed that in patient-derived tumor samples there are higher levels of Complex I-related gene expression compared to nontumor brain tissue. Because OXPHOS consumes O2, it can decrease tissue oxygenation and accordingly we found that DIPG tumors showed gene expression signatures reflective of hypoxia. Our animal models were also positive for markers of hypoxia in tumor regions, supporting the hypothesis that hypoxia is present in DIPG.

Mitochondria are often abnormal in cancer cells and targeting mitochondrial metabolism is a growing area of interest.25 Biguanides, typically used for diabetes, have been proposed as candidates for targeting mitochondria. Metformin has been linked to cancer prevention in retrospective clinical studies and shown to enhance response to anticancer therapeutics.26 It has also been used as a radiosensitizer in preclinical studies, including DIPGs.27,28 Metformin has also been shown to prolong survival in DIPG mouse models when combined with PI3K and protein kinase C inhibitors and radiation.29 Phenformin, as a more potent biguanide derivative, has radiosensitizing potential,30 but has been withdrawn from the market due to the risk of lactic acidosis31 warranting caution in any future proposed clinical use. Oxygenation plays an important role in the radiosensitivity of a tumor.32 Hypoxic cells require a 2- to 3-fold higher dose of irradiation to achieve the same cell killing effect as more well-oxygenated cells. Definitive evidence of hypoxia in DIPG is lacking but a recent study found elevated citrate levels, indicative of poor perfusion and hypoxia, in DIPG patients.7 Our research identified signatures of hypoxia in clinical cohorts of DIPG patients and orthotopic xenograft models. Phenformin alleviated hypoxia and reduced HIF-1α in DIPG neurospheres and our mouse models. Combining phenformin with radiation significantly prolonged survival in mice harboring DIPG tumors, with no obvious signs of toxicity in the animals, although blood lactate levels were not assessed. Interestingly, a recent study has reported that ONC201, a novel compound that targets and activates mitochondrial ATP-dependent caseinolytic peptidase P, has promise in treating DIPG patients.33 These findings highlight the potential of mitochondria in DIPG and its potential for ongoing drug development.

In vitro, we observed cells adapting to phenformin through alternative metabolic pathways, such as cholesterol synthesis and fatty acid pathways. Combining phenformin with statins or other metabolism-altering drugs, such as dichloroacetate,34 may enhance phenformin efficacy, and a recent preprint showed prolonged survival in animal models when combining phenformin with a statin.35 However, it is unknown whether this combination would radiosensitize. We also observed a phenformin radiosensitizing effect in the absence of hypoxia using 2D DIPG cultures, suggesting other underlying mechanisms of radiosensitization. DNA damage was only assessed at certain the timepoints; thus, it is unclear whether kinetics of DNA damage and repair are altered or whether more DNA damage is acquired with the combination treatment. Radiation can have immunostimulatory effects and biguanides have been shown to stimulate both the innate and adaptive immune systems9; therefore, in future, the combination should be tested in immunocompetent DIPG models.

In our current study, we did not explore the transcriptomic effect of combining phenformin with radiation due to the differing kinetics and biological effects of these treatments. Radiation’s impact unfolds over weeks, making clonogenic assays the standard for evaluating its efficacy, whereas drug treatments are typically assessed over 24-72 hours. Since the primary goal of this study was to investigate the radiosensitizing mechanism of a mitochondria-targeting drug, we focused on DIPG cells treated with phenformin for only 24 hours to study the resulting transcriptomic and metabolomic changes.

Although phenformin enhances DIPG radiosensitivity in vitro and the combination of radiation and phenformin prolongs survival in mouse models, the mice ultimately succumbed to their tumors. Additional combination therapies will likely be required to improve the efficacy of radiation. In this project, phenformin was used solely as a proof-of-concept experimental compound. While short-term use of phenformin, both alone and in combination with radiotherapy, did not show toxicity in a mouse model, its market withdrawal underscores the well-documented toxicity in human patients. Therefore, further investigation into its safety profile is essential before any consideration for clinical use. Other safer repurposed drugs with similar mechanisms of action may offer potential for radiosensitization in DIPG, and this could be explored in future studies. Although our clinical datasets show transcriptional signatures of hypoxia and increased Complex I gene expression, direct measurements of reduced oxygen levels and heightened mitochondrial activity in patients are still lacking. Other studies, including our own, have reported mitochondrial alterations in DIPG, such as decreased mitochondrial DNA.27 How these changes affect mitochondrial function or quantity in patient tumors remains unclear. Future studies should prioritize developing noninvasive methods to accurately assess these parameters. While our in vivo models demonstrated that phenformin plus radiation prolongs survival, we were unable to confirm whether the in vitro radiosensitizing mechanisms—namely hypoxia reduction and enhanced DNA damage—were also occurring in vivo. Phenformin may exert systemic metabolic effects that contribute to additional anticancer activity. Given phenformin’s safety profile, there are valid concerns about its use in a clinical setting. Our results demonstrate the potential of targeting mitochondria to reduce tumor hypoxia in DIPG. Furthermore, studies should explore whether safer drugs with similar mechanisms of action can be developed or whether mitochondrial inhibitors can be combined with other drugs to reduce the risk of lactic acidosis.
